coherence.reasons: Both run a clean hierarchy from governing thought to sections to slides, and both reach the same answer (Amazon-led, gated on ad cost, retail earned later). X's five-section flow is consistent, and its executive summary maps one-to-one to sections. Y's whether / route / how structure is tighter, and its slide 3 states the four conditions that must hold and gives a verdict on each, so every later slide has a clear job. X has one logical loose end: it says that above break-even ACoS "Japan becomes the better 2027 choice" and gates on "switch to Japan", but ACoS at scale can only be observed after the 2027 slot is spent. Y closes that gap by arguing that waiting would not resolve the unknown and that a red gate frees the 2028 slot for Japan. Y's amber gate (accept a payback slip) sits in some tension with "the only route within the board's limits", but Y flags it as a departure for the board to decide.

judgment.reasons: Both land on the key's preferred recommendation (R1) and compare A, B and J on the board's cap, payback and margin floor. Y weighs the trade-offs more squarely. It states that no route reaches $40M by 2030 within the limits and asks the board to restate the ambition. It admits that at the 32% benchmark the payback is missed, and asks the board to pre-agree whether a slip to 2031–32 is acceptable. It says Japan returns more four-year cash unless ACoS stays below about 26%, and it explains why delaying the US does not buy information. Its green / amber / red gate thresholds are derived from the model (28.6% payback break-even, 34.4% zero 2029 operating profit), with a tariff adjustment. It adds a 12-month door test at 4.0 units or more before any retail roll-out. X's five gates, owners and risk table are solid, and its ACoS gate stays strictly on the board's payback constraint. But X treats the $40M gap mainly as "a matter of timing" flagged in a footnote, and its Japan fallback is less worked through.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the key numbers correctly: $4.73 and $7.55 unit contributions, Option B peak of −$20.8M and 4.5% group margin in 2027, break-even ACoS of 28.6%, cumulative cash of +$2.4M / +$0.4M / −$2.3M at 25% / 28% / 32% ACoS, and Japan at +$1.8M. Both check 4.5 units per door against the 2.6 median and the 4.0 delisting line, reject the $5.2B figure, and challenge the 0.71 correlation. X has the more explicit ACoS-by-tariff grid (28% ACoS with 25% duty gives −$0.7M) and the fuller treatment of the correlation (reverse cause, common cause, and not decisive even if real). Y adds a volume-by-ACoS grid, ten stress cases, the halo and sell-through B would need to pay back (3.1×, 23.5 units), B at realistic inputs (−$26.4M), the tariff-adjusted break-even (27.0%), and a run-rate check on the 300,000-unit plan. Y also uses CAGRs (17.3% against 5.1%). X makes a few unsupported inferences: "US buyers rate it as Korean buyers do" (no Korean rating is in the pack), steady growth as "a sign of word of mouth", and "the pilot understates what a full range can do". Y's survivorship handling ("two of three stalled") is a little more explicit.

revision.reasons: Both keep the CEO's Amazon-first hypothesis with conditions, which is the handling the key expects. Both raise the retail awareness trigger from 15% to 20% using the Table 8 bands, and both replace the assumed 25% ACoS with a gate at the 28.6% break-even. X has a clear from/to slide with three changes. Y goes further in three ways. It breaks the hypothesis into four testable conditions with a verdict on each. It keeps the $10M Amazon trigger and adds a door test, turning the 2029 date into an option to be earned. It also resets the $40M ambition in so many words ("$25M+ by 2030, on a path to $40M by ~2032"), which the key names as part of a good answer. X only flags the reading of the ambition for the board to confirm.

overall.reasons: The two documents are close: same recommendation, same core numbers, and both test the planning assumptions against the benchmarks. Y would serve the board somewhat better. It turns the analysis into five explicit board decisions and is candid that payback is likely missed at benchmark ad cost, asking the board to decide in advance how to treat that. It states the ambition-versus-constraints trade-off outright and resolves the timing logic of the Japan alternative. Its sensitivity work is broader (volume, top-of-range ACoS, what B would need to pay back). X is thorough and accurate, with a stronger tariff grid and correlation critique, but it is softer on the $40M reset, has a few unsupported inferences, and offers a less coherent "switch to Japan" fallback.
